title: Reactions of acids with metals, bases and carbonates

tips.title: The acid names the salt
tips.body: **Hydrochloric** acid makes a **chloride**, **nitric** acid makes a **nitrate**, **sulfuric** acid makes a **sulfate**. The **positive ion** in the base gives the first word, and it is nearly always a **metal**. So magnesium oxide plus sulfuric acid can only be **magnesium sulfate** — you never have to guess a product.

tips.title: Three reactions, three product lists
tips.body: Acid + **metal** → **salt + hydrogen**. Acid + **base or alkali** → **salt + water**. Acid + **carbonate** → **salt + water + carbon dioxide**. The carbonate is the only one giving **three** products, and it is the only one that fizzes with a gas that turns limewater milky.

tips.title: A base is not always an alkali
tips.body: A **base** neutralises an acid. An **alkali** is a base that **dissolves in water**. So all alkalis are bases, but a base such as **copper(II) oxide** is insoluble and is not an alkali. Questions use both words deliberately.

tips.title: Neutralisation is one ionic equation
tips.body:
$$\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$$

Every acid-alkali neutralisation is this reaction, whichever acid and whichever alkali. If you can write it, you can explain why the pH moves towards 7.

tips.title: pH 7 is neutral, and the scale runs 0 to 14
tips.body: **Below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline.** Universal indicator gives an **approximate** pH by colour; a **pH probe** gives a number. A question asking for an accurate value wants the probe.

why.matters:
An acid is not a substance with a temper. It is a supply of **hydrogen ions**, and everything acids do follows from what those ions do — which is why one ionic equation, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, covers every neutralisation there is.

The rest of the topic is the payoff. Three reactions with three product lists, and a naming rule that fixes the salt from the acid and the metal. Between them you can predict the products of a reaction you have never seen, which is exactly what the specification asks you to do.

examples.title: Why an indigestion tablet fizzes
examples.body:
A stomach makes hydrochloric acid, and when there is too much of it an antacid is a **base** — usually a carbonate or a hydroxide — that neutralises the excess.

Which one it is decides what you notice. A carbonate gives salt, water **and carbon dioxide**, so the tablet fizzes in the glass and the gas has to go somewhere afterwards. A hydroxide gives salt and water only, and nothing fizzes. Counting the products tells you which kind of base is in the packet.

visual.alt: Two balanced equations side by side: a carbonate antacid with stomach acid giving a salt, water and carbon dioxide, and a hydroxide antacid giving a salt and water with no gas at all

examples.title: Reading the salt off the label
examples.body:
Calcium chloride is spread on roads, ammonium nitrate is sold by the sack as fertiliser, and magnesium sulfate is the Epsom salts in a bath. Three names on three shelves, and each one says which acid it was made from.

The acid fixes the second word — chloride, nitrate, sulfate — and the metal fixes the first. That is why you never have to guess a salt: given zinc oxide and sulfuric acid, the only answer available is zinc sulfate.

examples.title: What a pH reading is actually counting
examples.body:
A pool kit, a soil kit and a strip of universal indicator all report the same thing: how many **hydrogen ions** are in the solution. Below 7 there is an excess of H⁺, above 7 an excess of OH⁻, and at 7 they balance.

That is why the numbers on a household shelf run the way they do, from lemon juice at the acid end to oven cleaner at the other. It is also why the indicator colour is only an estimate: a colour is judged by eye, and a probe gives a number.

visual.alt: A table of everyday pH values running from lemon juice at two and vinegar at about two point four, through pure water at seven, to baking soda solution at nine and oven cleaner at thirteen

steps.title: Acids with metals
steps.body:
**Acids react with some metals to produce salts and hydrogen.**

$$\text{acid} + \text{metal} \rightarrow \text{salt} + \text{hydrogen}$$

**The spec limits what you need**: the reactions of **magnesium, zinc and iron** with **hydrochloric** and **sulfuric** acids. So there are six reactions, and they all follow the same pattern.

$$\mathrm{Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2}$$

$$\mathrm{Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2}$$

**What you see** is the metal disappearing and **bubbles of gas**. The gas is **hydrogen**, and it is identified by a **burning splint**, which makes it burn rapidly with a **squeaky pop**.

**The more reactive the metal, the faster the fizzing** — magnesium reacts vigorously, zinc steadily, iron slowly. That is a first look at the reactivity series, which comes later in this unit.

**Higher tier: these are redox reactions.** The metal **loses electrons**, so it is **oxidised**; the hydrogen ions **gain electrons**, so they are **reduced**.

$$\mathrm{Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

$$\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}$$

The metal atom becomes a positive ion, which is the same idea that orders the whole reactivity series.

steps.title: Acids with bases, alkalis and carbonates
steps.body:
**Acids are neutralised by alkalis and bases to produce salts and water, and by metal carbonates to produce salts, water and carbon dioxide.**

$$\text{acid} + \text{base} \rightarrow \text{salt} + \text{water}$$

$$\text{acid} + \text{metal carbonate} \rightarrow \text{salt} + \text{water} + \text{carbon dioxide}$$

**Bases and alkalis are not the same word twice.** A **base** is anything that neutralises an acid — typically a **metal oxide** or **metal hydroxide**. An **alkali** is a base that **dissolves in water**. So sodium hydroxide is a base *and* an alkali; **copper(II) oxide** is a base but **not** an alkali, because it is insoluble.

**Examples:**

$$\mathrm{2HCl + CuO \rightarrow CuCl_2 + H_2O}$$

$$\mathrm{H_2SO_4 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + 2H_2O}$$

$$\mathrm{2HCl + CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaCl_2 + H_2O + CO_2}$$

**The carbonate reaction is the one you can recognise instantly**, because it **fizzes** and the gas turns **limewater milky** — the test for carbon dioxide. A metal oxide dissolving in acid does not fizz at all.

steps.title: Naming the salt
steps.body:
**You are expected to predict products from given reactants**, and the naming rule makes that mechanical.

**The acid decides the second word:**

- **hydrochloric** acid → a **chloride**
- **nitric** acid → a **nitrate**
- **sulfuric** acid → a **sulfate**

**The positive ion in the base decides the first word** — nearly always a metal, and ammonium in an ammonium salt. Put the two together and the salt names itself.

steps.title: The pH scale and neutralisation
steps.body:
**Acids produce hydrogen ions, $\mathrm{H^+}$, in aqueous solution. Aqueous solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions, $\mathrm{OH^-}$.** Those two ions are what the whole pH scale is about.

**The pH scale runs from 0 to 14** and measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is:

- **below 7** — **acidic**
- **exactly 7** — **neutral**
- **above 7** — **alkaline**

**How to measure it.** **Universal indicator** changes colour and gives an **approximate** pH by matching against a chart. A **pH probe** gives a **numerical** value and is more accurate. A question asking for an accurate pH wants the probe; a question asking to show a colour change wants the indicator.

**What neutralisation actually is.** In a reaction between an acid and an alkali, **hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to produce water**:

$$\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$$

**This single equation is every acid-alkali neutralisation there is.** Whichever acid and whichever alkali, it is always these two ions combining. The metal ion and the acid's negative ion stay in solution as the **salt** and take no part — they are spectator ions.

So as alkali is added to an acid, $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions are used up, the concentration falls, and the **pH rises towards 7**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The salt is predictable, so never guess it.** The **acid** fixes the second word — chloride, nitrate, sulfate — and the **metal** fixes the first. This works for a reactant pair you have never seen, which is exactly what *predict the products from given reactants* is asking for.

**Count the products to identify the reaction.** Two products with a gas that **pops** means a **metal**. Two products and **no gas** means a **base or alkali**. **Three** products with a gas that turns **limewater milky** means a **carbonate**. An experiment that gives you the observations is asking you to run this backwards.

**Neutralisation is one equation, not many.** $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$ happens whichever acid meets whichever alkali, because the salt ions are **spectators**. Saying that explicitly — that the metal ion and the acid anion take no part — is what separates a described answer from an explained one.

**Base and alkali are not synonyms.** Every **alkali** is a **base**; a base is only an alkali if it **dissolves in water**. **Copper(II) oxide** is the standard example of a base that is not an alkali, and it is why the soluble-salt preparation in the next topic can use an insoluble solid at all.

**Higher tier: acid and metal reactions are redox.** The metal **loses electrons** and is **oxidised**; the **hydrogen ions gain electrons** and are **reduced**. Writing the two half equations and checking they add to the overall reaction with the electrons cancelling is the strongest form of that answer.

**Universal indicator and a pH probe answer different questions.** The indicator shows a **colour** and gives an approximate value, useful for showing a change. The probe gives a **number** and is what you use when accuracy matters. Choosing the right one, and saying why, is a routine two-mark exchange.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen.** Limited to **magnesium, zinc and iron** with **hydrochloric** and **sulfuric** acids.
- **Acid + base or alkali → salt + water.**
- **Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide** — the only one with **three** products.
- A **base** neutralises an acid; an **alkali** is a base that **dissolves in water**.
- **Copper(II) oxide** is a base but **not** an alkali, because it is insoluble.
- **Hydrochloric** acid → **chloride**. **Nitric** acid → **nitrate**. **Sulfuric** acid → **sulfate**.
- The **metal** in the base gives the first word of the salt.
- **Hydrogen** is tested with a **burning splint**: it burns with a **pop**.
- **Carbon dioxide** turns **limewater milky**.
- Acids produce **$\mathrm{H^+}$** ions in solution; alkalis contain **$\mathrm{OH^-}$** ions.
- The **pH scale runs 0 to 14**: below 7 **acidic**, 7 **neutral**, above 7 **alkaline**.
- **Universal indicator** gives an approximate pH by colour; a **pH probe** gives a number.
- Neutralisation is $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$, the same for **every** acid and alkali.
- The salt ions are **spectators** and take no part.
- **Higher tier**: acid and metal reactions are **redox** — the metal is **oxidised**, the hydrogen ions are **reduced**.

questions.prompt: A student has three unlabelled solids: a metal, a metal oxide and a metal carbonate. Describe how reacting each with dilute hydrochloric acid would let them be identified, and give the products in each case.
questions.solution:
Adding dilute hydrochloric acid to each solid separates them in one step, because the **number of products** and the **gas given off** differ in all three cases.

The **metal** would **fizz**, because an acid reacting with a metal produces a **salt and hydrogen**. The gas can be identified by holding a **burning splint** at the mouth of the tube: hydrogen burns rapidly with a **squeaky pop**. The metal would gradually disappear as it reacted.

The **metal carbonate** would also **fizz**, so fizzing alone does not identify it — the gas has to be tested. Bubbling it through **limewater** turns the limewater **milky**, which identifies **carbon dioxide**. An acid with a carbonate gives **three** products: a salt, water **and** carbon dioxide, and it is the only one of the three reactions that does.

The **metal oxide** would **not fizz at all**. A metal oxide is a **base**, and an acid with a base gives only a **salt and water**. The solid would simply dissolve as it reacted, often with the solution taking on a colour if the metal is a transition metal.

Because the acid used is **hydrochloric**, all three salts would be **chlorides** — the acid always fixes the second word of the salt's name, and the metal in the solid fixes the first. Had nitric acid been used the products would have been nitrates, and sulfuric acid would have given sulfates, with the rest of the reasoning unchanged.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens, in terms of ions, when hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide solution, and explain why the same ionic equation describes every acid and alkali neutralisation.
questions.solution:
Hydrochloric acid in solution produces **hydrogen ions, $\mathrm{H^+}$**, together with chloride ions. Sodium hydroxide solution, being an **alkali**, contains **hydroxide ions, $\mathrm{OH^-}$**, together with sodium ions.

When the two are mixed, the reaction that actually happens is between those two ions alone:

$$\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$$

The **hydrogen ions react with the hydroxide ions to produce water**. Meanwhile the **sodium ions** and the **chloride ions** are still dissolved, and they are still dissolved afterwards — they have not reacted with anything. They are **spectator ions**. They form the **salt**, sodium chloride, which is why evaporating the solution afterwards leaves solid salt behind.

As alkali is added, more and more $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions are used up, so the **concentration of hydrogen ions falls**, and the **pH rises towards 7**. At exactly the point where the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions are present in equal amounts, the solution is **neutral**.

The reason the same equation describes **every** acid–alkali neutralisation is that the spectator ions never appear in it. Whichever acid is used, it supplies $\mathrm{H^+}$; whichever alkali is used, it supplies $\mathrm{OH^-}$; and those are the only two species that change. The identity of the acid and the alkali decides **which salt** is left in solution, but it does not change the reaction taking place. That is why one short ionic equation can stand for a whole class of reactions — and why being able to write it is worth more than memorising a list of word equations.

examTechnique.body:
This topic rewards **pattern rather than recall**. Three reactions, each with its own product list, and a naming rule that lets you predict a salt you have never met. Learn the three product lists as a set, and name every salt in two moves: the acid gives the ending, the positive ion (usually a metal) gives the first word.

The observations are half the marks. A gas that **pops** is hydrogen and means a **metal**; a gas that turns **limewater milky** is carbon dioxide and means a **carbonate**; **no gas** means a **base**.
examinerErrors: Giving **two** products for an acid and a **carbonate**, when there are **three**.
Using **base** and **alkali** as if they meant the same thing.
Guessing a salt name rather than taking the ending from the **acid**.
Saying a reaction fizzes without **testing the gas**, so a metal and a carbonate are not distinguished.
Writing the neutralisation equation with the **salt ions included**, rather than as $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$.
Choosing **universal indicator** when the question asks for an **accurate** pH.
Forgetting that acid and metal reactions are limited to **magnesium, zinc and iron** with **hydrochloric and sulfuric** acids.
Saying magnesium is **reduced** in an acid reaction, when it **loses** electrons and is **oxidised**.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer predicts rather than recalls. Given an unfamiliar acid and base it names the salt in two moves and says why. Given observations it runs the logic backwards — three products and milky limewater can only be a **carbonate**. On neutralisation it writes $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$ and then explains the part most answers leave out: the salt ions are **spectators**, which is precisely why one equation covers every acid and every alkali. At Higher tier it treats acid and metal reactions as **redox**, writes both half equations, and checks they add to the overall reaction with the electrons cancelling.
